planting.note: Set container-grown plants out in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil, giving this eventual small tree plenty of room to broaden into its mature pyramidal shape.

directions: Squarrosa is one of the oldest named Sawara cypress selections, retaining its soft, juvenile, awl-shaped foliage indefinitely instead of maturing to the flattened adult sprays typical of the species, giving the whole plant a fuzzy, silvery blue-gray, moss-like texture. Growth is slow to moderate, building over decades into a broad, informally pyramidal small tree rather than staying dwarf, so it suits larger borders, specimen use, or mixed conifer collections more than tight foundation plantings. Plant in full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained soil, since the fine juvenile foliage can brown in prolonged drought or waterlogged ground alike. It needs little pruning beyond removing any reverted branches showing coarser adult-type foliage, which should be cut out to preserve the soft mossy character.

common_name: Plumosa Aurea Sawara Cypress (Golden Plume Falsecypress)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun and well-drained soil so the feathery gold foliage colors up fully before the first winter.

directions: Plumosa Aurea is a Victorian-era Sawara cypress selection prized for its soft, feathery, plume-like juvenile foliage that emerges bright golden-yellow on new growth and mellows to a yellow-green through the rest of the season. It builds slowly into a broad, informally conical small tree over many years, useful as a specimen or accent where its warm color can contrast with darker evergreens. Full sun brings out the strongest gold tone, though the foliage can bronze or scorch in reflected heat during peak summer in hot regions; even, well-drained moisture keeps the fine sprays from browning. Prune out any shoots that revert to coarser green adult foliage to keep the plume-like texture and color consistent throughout the crown.

common_name: Echiniformis Hedgehog Spruce (Dwarf Globe White Spruce)

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring in gritty, well-drained soil; this cultivar's extreme slowness makes it best suited to rock gardens, troughs, and other spots where it will not be crowded out by faster neighbors.

directions: Echiniformis is a classic 19th-century dwarf white spruce cultivar that forms a dense, gray-green globe of short, stiff, prickly needles, advancing only a fraction of an inch in height and width most years. Its bun-like, congested habit makes it a long-lived centerpiece for alpine troughs, rock gardens, and miniature conifer collections rather than a general landscape shrub. Grow in full sun in gritty, well-drained soil, since poor drainage and deep shade both weaken its tight, globose form over time. It needs no routine pruning or shaping, and established plants tolerate cold winters and brief dry spells without complaint.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, where its congested branching can be appreciated up close in a rock garden or conifer bed.

directions: Ohlendorffii is an old German dwarf Norway spruce selection, dating to the early twentieth century, valued for its dense, irregularly mounded habit built from short, tightly crowded branchlets. New growth emerges pale yellow-green to gold-tipped in spring before settling into deep green, giving the plant seasonal two-tone interest against its darker interior foliage. It grows slowly into an asymmetric, somewhat lumpy dome that adds textural contrast in rock gardens, dwarf conifer collections, and mixed evergreen beds. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade and skip routine pruning, since its naturally irregular outline is part of its appeal.

planting.note: Set out in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; being one of the slowest dwarf spruce cultivars, it is best given a permanent, uncrowded spot in a rock garden or trough.

directions: Gregoryana is among the oldest recorded dwarf Norway spruce cultivars, forming a dense, flat-topped cushion or bun of tightly packed, radiating branches clothed in short, stiff, dark green needles. Its growth rate is extremely slow, often only an inch or two per year, so it remains a compact, long-lived accent for rock gardens, troughs, and dwarf conifer collections for many decades. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, since dense shade thins the cushion form and encourages looser, less characteristic growth. It requires no shearing or shaping, as the plant's naturally tight, mounded silhouette is the main reason it has stayed popular for over a century.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; like other junipers it needs sharp drainage and resents wet feet.

directions: Meyer's Blue Juniper was introduced from China by plant explorer Frank Meyer in the early twentieth century and remains one of the most vividly silvery-blue junipers grown, with dense, prickly, awl-shaped foliage covering an irregular, often sprawling branch structure. Left unstaked it forms a loose, informal mound, while many gardeners train a leader upward to create a small accent tree with cascading side branches. It is considerably more vigorous and less tidy than its compact sport, Blue Star Juniper, and needs occasional selective pruning to control wayward, fast-growing shoots and keep an attractive shape. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, where it tolerates heat, drought, and poor rocky ground far better than damp or heavy clay conditions.
